---
title: "Part II"
---

In the second part of this book, we demonstrate how to conduct a priori power analyses using R packages and simulation-based approaches. This section begins with simple research designs, including paired- and unpaired-sample designs, moves on to factorial designs, then briefly covers equivalence tests and concludes with simple multilevel models. For readers interested in a hands-on introduction using JAMOVI, we recommend [Power to the People: A Beginner’s Tutorial to Power Analysis using jamovi](https://open.lnu.se/index.php/metapsychology/article/view/3078) [@bartlett_jamovi]. For readers interested in a hands-on introduction using G\*Power, we recommend [Introduction to sample size calculation using G\*Power](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&opi=89978449&url=https://files.osf.io/v1/resources/pcfvj/providers/osfstorage/5dcea84d5b97bd000e57aba0%3Faction%3Ddownload%26version%3D1%26direct&ved=2ahUKEwjtgZuoiPmNAxVMhv0HHV1ADNcQFnoECBsQAQ&usg=AOvVaw2CLKMTGddzS9qyMWaGJMmA).

To estimate the power for factorial designs, researchers can use the package `Superpower` to set up the factorial design using `ANOVA_design()` and perform the simulations and analyses of main and interaction effects, as well as planned pairwise comparisons, using `ANOVA_power()`. A comprehensive tutorial on using `Superpower` package can be found in [Power Analysis with Superpower](https://aaroncaldwell.us/SuperpowerBook/).

Another approach to power analysis is by conducting simulations. A key advantage of simulation-based approaches is their flexibility. They allow researchers to explore how different assumptions (e.g., size of the effect, correlation between measurements) or analytic decisions (e.g., include or not a covariate) affect power. This makes simulation especially useful in complex study designs where analytic formulas are limited or unavailable. Briefly, simulation involves repeatedly simulating data and performing the relevant statistical test to estimate power. To simulate data we will be using the `faux::sim_design()`. For a comprehensive tutorial on using `faux` package, readers are referred to <https://debruine.github.io/faux/index.html>. For a gentle introduction to conducting a power analysis using simulations, readers are also referred to [Nick's post](https://nickch-k.github.io/EconometricsSlides/Week_08/Power_Simulations.html) and [LMU Open Science Center](https://lmu-osc.github.io/Simulations-for-Advanced-Power-Analyses/LM1.html).

::: callout-important
The basic steps of the more flexible form of simulation-based approach are:

-   Simulate data with the desired properties (e.g., group means and standard deviations).

-   Perform the planned statistical test on the simulated data.

-   Extract the resulting *p*-value.

-   Repeat this process many times (e.g., 1,000 simulations).

-   Store the results.

-   Calculate power as the proportion of *p*-values that fall below $\alpha$.
:::
